sections.title: A repeated event is not yet an explanation

paragraphs.text: A pattern is a recurring relationship between actions and circumstances. Similar memories can suggest one without establishing its cause. Comparing occasions means checking what repeats, what changes and what might distinguish explanations. It is reasoning under uncertainty, not a test that reads intentions.

Painful or memorable events can dominate an account. Once you adopt a label, matching events may stand out while exceptions fade. A short record near the event can preserve your original observation, but it remains your perspective and may omit something another person knows.

Saul Shiffman and colleagues reviewed repeated sampling of experiences close to the time they occur. This can reduce reliance on global retrospective reports. An ordinary notebook is not a validated assessment or proof of cause. Recording should remain proportionate and must not become surveillance.

Choose a narrow question, such as when a particular kind of help is declined, rather than what kind of person someone is. Include opportunities when the response could have happened but did not. Not observing something is different from knowing it was absent.

In a fictional example, your father declines help with finances but accepts lifts and help carrying bags. This weakens the claim that he refuses all help. Decision ownership, privacy and the nature of the task become worth checking; the contrast does not prove any of those explanations.

Repetition can reflect constraints, habits, expectations or deliberate influence. Shared behaviour across relatives does not separate genetics from learning. One serious act can also warrant action; you do not need a complete pattern before seeking support.

sections.title: Use a modest prediction and a safe action

paragraphs.text: Choose a respectful clarification or small reversible change within your control. State what you expect it might clarify and what would make you reconsider. Keep the original account and add later learning instead of rewriting the past to fit your current view.

Aaron Fisher and colleagues highlighted difficulties transferring aggregate patterns to individual processes. That is a reason to examine context, not to discard population research. Benjamin Harkin and colleagues found benefits from monitoring progress toward goals, but that evidence did not test surveillance or this book’s complete method.

Stop if tracking becomes rumination, surveillance or a barrier to making a practical decision. Keep identifying detail to what is needed. Several retellings of one event remain one occasion, and an AI restating your report is not another source.

sections.title: Decide what to retain, change or stop

paragraphs.text: Think of one occasion and a genuine comparison. Can you name two plausible explanations and something that would weaken each? Pause for longer if useful.

For the help example, a question about financial privacy might distinguish the task from help in general. It should not be a demand for access to private information or a hidden experiment on the person.

When you can write, record the observation, comparison, competing explanations, safe action and review date. At review, include costs, unintended effects and remaining uncertainty. Choose what to retain, change or stop rather than scoring someone’s character.
